correctedText:
Beverly Kerecman has spent decades preserving Japanese American culture in Cleveland while building a career in special education, literacy, and teacher development. Born Beverly Haru Hashiguchi in Cleveland and a graduate of Cleveland Heights High School, she earned a degree in Special Education from Kent State University and later advanced degrees in reading, literacy, and teacher leadership.

Her family’s Cleveland story began with displacement. During World War II, both sides of her family were incarcerated in Japanese American internment camps after losing homes, businesses, and livelihoods in California. After the war, they were among the Japanese Americans who resettled in the Cleveland area. Her parents later met through the Cleveland Nisei Tennis Club.

Growing up in postwar Cleveland, Kerecman became part of a Japanese American community that had created its own social, athletic, religious, and cultural institutions. As a young person, she joined the ShoJoJi Japanese Dancers, supported by the Cleveland Chapter of the Japanese American Citizens League. During college, she and Nanci Taketa assumed leadership of the group, continuing its mission to preserve and share Japanese dance in Northeast Ohio.

Kerecman has carried that tradition into new generations. She coordinated Cleveland’s Obon Festival, bringing together the ShoJoJi Japanese Dancers, Cleveland Japanese American Citizens League, and Cleveland Japanese American Foundation. Rooted in Buddhist tradition, Obon honors ancestors while creating a public gathering around music, dance, memory, and heritage.

Her work with the Japanese American Citizens League has joined cultural preservation with civil and human rights. As an officer in both the Cleveland JACL and Junior JACL, she organized programs about the World War II incarceration of Japanese Americans, brought speakers and workshops to local audiences, created youth programs, contributed to the JACL newsletter, and served on its scholarship committee.

Kerecman has also served as President of Cleveland Asian Retired Persons and volunteered with the Cleveland International Film Festival, extending her involvement across the region’s broader Asian American cultural life.

Professionally, Kerecman worked as an intervention specialist in the Mayfield City Schools and Shaker Heights School System, served for ten years as an adjunct instructor at Notre Dame College, and trained educators in literacy instruction. Her accomplishments include National Board Certification, leadership with the Ohio Council for Exceptional Children, and recognition for her work in education.

Beverly Kerecman’s Cleveland legacy lies in preserving Japanese American memory while strengthening the institutions that carry it forward. Through ShoJoJi, Obon, civil-rights programs, youth activities, and decades of civic involvement, she has helped keep Japanese American history and culture visible in Cleveland’s public life.
note: Her biography used her birth name, Hashiguchi, as her surname throughout and never the name she was inducted under. It now calls her Kerecman and says once that she was born Beverly Haru Hashiguchi, as the Hall of Fame's own text records; nothing else changed. At Tony Yanick's request.
